## **Problem**
I’m unable to install a package if its root/default branch is named `master` instead of `main`.  
The package manager appears to assume that the default branch is always `main`, causing installations to fail for repositories that use `master` or any other branch name.

## **Proposed Solution**
Allow specifying the branch name in `apm.yml` under the `dependencies.apm` block.

Example:

```yml
dependencies:
  apm:
    namespace/repo-name: branch-name
```

This would
[Middle omitted to fit model context]

As a result, reusing configurations across repos (and building MCP-style collections like Jira/Confluence) is hard, and the central format maintained by APM isn’t leveraged consistently for cross-repo references.

It does not deploy agents or skills from `apm_modules/` into `.claude/agents/` or `.claude/skills/`. These primitives are left stranded in `apm_modules/` and never reach Claude Code's native discovery directories.

## Current behavior

```

apm compile       → merges instructions → CLAUDE.md

**Match the output format to how the target platform actually consumes it.** Claude Code consumes agents as files in a directory, not as blocks in a markdown document. Compile should respect that.

Title: [FEATURE] Support Hooks as an Agent Primitive
Body: Hooks are supported both by GitHub Copilot (e.g. in [VSCode](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/copilot/customization/hooks)) and [Claude Code](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks).

Title: [FEATURE] Bitbucket Cloud support
Body: ## Summary

APM currently supports GitHub and Azure DevOps as package sources. Bitbucket Cloud is another widely used platform.

## Scope

- **Bitbucket Cloud** (bitbucket.org)
- Note: Bitbucket uses `workspace/repo` instead of `owner/repo`

## Implementation approach

This will be addressed via generic git URL support in #72 rather than a Bitbucket-specific API integration. Supporting `https://bitbucket.org/workspace/repo.git` as a dependency reference in `apm.yml` avoids the need for Bitbucket REST API v2 integration and handles the `workspace/repo` convention naturally.

```yaml
dependencies:
  apm:
    - https://bitbucket.org/acme/design-standards.git
```

Authentication works via standard git credential helpers (SSH keys, credential managers) — no `BITBUCKET_APM_TOKEN` env var needed.

Title: Content security scanning for prompt files (hidden Unicode detection)
Body: ## Problem

Shared prompt and instruction files (`.cursorrules`, `.github/prompts/`, etc.) are becoming a de facto supply chain — but without any integrity guarantees. Researchers [found that 6 of 50 popular shared `.cursorrules` files](https://agentseal.org/blog/cursor-rules-hidden-instructions) contained hidden zero-width Unicode characters embedded between visible text.

These characters are invisible to humans but LLMs tokenize them individually, meaning models can process instructions developers cannot see. Some had patterns consistent with deliberate instruction embedding using Unicode tag characters (U+E0001–U+E007F), which map 1:1 to invisible
[Middle omitted to fit model context]
 |

### Product positioning

This is the first pillar of `apm audit`. Future modes include `--ci` (lock consistency) and `--drift` (on-disk divergence), as documented in the [governance guide](https://microsoft.github.io/apm/enterprise/governance/).

Title: Content integrity hashing in lockfile (SHA-256)
Body: ## Summary

Title: Harden SSH URL path validation against traversal sequences
Body: ## Description

During review of #437, we identified that SSH-style URL parsing in `DependencyReference` (`src/apm_cli/models/dependency/reference.py`) does not apply the same path component validation as HTTPS URLs.

## Current behavior

HTTPS URLs validate each path component against `[a-zA-Z0-9._-]+` and reject `..` traversal sequences. SSH URLs (`git@host:owner/repo`) bypass some of these checks.

## Expected behavior

Both URL parsing paths should apply identical path traversal protections.

## Location

- `src/apm_cli/models/dependency/reference.py` -- SSH URL parsing branch
- Related: #437 (ADO spaces fix, where this was noticed)

## Impact

Low severity -- APM already validates paths downstream, but defense-in-depth dictates validating at parse time too.

Title: perf: `apm deps update` re-downloads packages even when SHA is unchanged
Body: ## Problem

`apm deps update` delegates to `_install_apm_dependencies(update_refs=True)`, which correctly re-resolves git refs to their latest commit SHAs (API call). However, when the resolved SHA matches the existing lockfile SHA, the engine still:

1. **Re-clones/fetches** the package (unnecessary network + I/O)
2. **Re-integrates** all primitives (unnecessary file writes)
3. **Re-computes** content hashes (unnecessary CPU)

This happens because `update_refs
[Middle omitted to fit model context]
-downloads and re-integrates everything. With this optimization, it would only make lightweight API calls to verify SHAs, making the common case (nothing changed) near-instant.

## Context

Discovered during E2E testing of PR #493. The update command works correctly -- this is purely a performance optimization.

Title: Inconsistent file extensions between apm.yml and apm.lock.yaml
Body: ## Summary

APM currently uses:
- `apm.yml` for the manifest
- `apm.lock.yaml` for the lockfile

These two files are both YAML-based, but use different file extensions (`.yml` vs `.yaml`), which feels inconsistent.

## Problem

This inconsistency can be slightly confusing for users, especially since both files are:

- YAML 1.2 documents
- Core project configuration files
- Expected to be committed to version control

Most ecosystems tend to keep naming consistent across manifest and lockfile (e.g. `package.json` /
[Middle omitted to fit model context]
per lockfile spec).
- However, the choice of `.yaml` over `.yml`, and the inconsistency with `apm.yml`, is not explained in the current documentation.

## Question

Was this inconsistency intentional?

If not, would you consider aligning the extensions for better consistency and developer experience?

Title: Local relative paths in transitive deps resolve against root consumer instead of declaring package

Relative paths in a non-root package's `apm.yml` are resolved against the **root consumer's** project directory rather than the package's **own source directory**. This makes it impossible to compose two local sibling packages where one declares the other as a dependency — the natural pattern for layering reusable building blocks inside a single repo.

The fix is small (~30 LOC), aligns APM with the semantics every other package manager (npm, pip, cargo, go modules, Bicep) uses for relative paths in manifests, and unlocks clean local-package composition without changing the common case.

Title: Bug: apm install --mcp without --transport fails with AttributeError
Body: ## Description

`apm install --mcp <registry-ref>` without `--transport` fails with:

```
'str' object has no attribute 'get'
```

The code path expects the MCP dependency to be a dict (with `.get()`), but when a bare registry reference string is passed without `--transport`, it remains a `str`.

## Reproduce

```bash
apm install --mcp io.github.github/github-mcp-server
```

## Workaround

Specify `--transport` explicitly:

```bash
apm install --mcp io.github.github/github-mcp-server --transport stdio
```

## Expected behavior

`apm install --mcp <ref>` should either infer a default transport or provide a clear error asking the user to specify one.

## Affected versions

Observed on 0.10.0. Affects all targets (not Gemini-specific).

Title: [BUG] Parallel sparse-checkout race condition when two subdirectory deps reference the same repository
Body: **Describe the bug**

When an `apm.yml` declares two (or more) virtual subdirectory dependencies that reference **the same GitHub repository** (e.g. `org/repo/shared` and `org/repo/plugins`), the parallel resolution introduced in v0.12.1 causes a race condition. Both dependencies attempt to sparse-checkout the same cloned repo concurrently, but only one subdirectory path is configured — the other always fails with:

```
Failed to download dependency <org>/<repo>: Subdirectory '<subdir>' not found in repository
```

Each subdirectory
[Middle omitted to fit model context]
 configured the sparse-checkout cone for only its own path.
- **Workaround:** Run `apm install` twice — the first run populates the clone cache, and the second succeeds. Alternatively, restructure to use a single root-level `.apm/` directory so consumers only need one dependency entry per repository.

Title: RFE: Extend brownfield discovery to cover agent harness (hooks, commands, styles)

Extends `apm init --discover` (#1122) to inventory the full agent **harness** alongside instructions, agents, and skills. The harness covers the runtime execution wrappers that tools use to trigger scripts, expose slash commands, and enforce output style.

## Motivation

When migrating between agent tools (e.g. Claude to Codex), teams also need to migrate their hooks, custom commands, and style guides -- not just their instruction files. Discovery should surface all of these so the proposed `apm.yml` reflects the complete picture.

## Proposed additions to discovery

For **cross-cutting substrate plugins** that act as a *floor* (e.g. a `secure-baseline` shipping security instructions + a security reviewer persona that every consumer must inherit), first-wins is dangerous: a phase-kit plugin upgrade that bumps its transitive ref of
[Middle omitted to fit model context]

Title: [FEATURE] Add package registry support for dependency resolution
Body: **Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**
APM currently resolves dependencies primarily through Git-based references. While this works well for repository-based packages, enterprise teams also need a first-class way to distribute private packages through existing artifact infrastructure, authenticate registry access, verify downloaded artifacts, and integrate with standard package governance workflows.

Teams should also be able to use semver-based version selection when it fits their release process, without forcing all registry-published package versions to be semver. Many organizations already use Git-flow style selectors such as main, stable, v1.0.0, promotion labels, or commit-like pins,
[Middle omitted to fit model context]
 why it is proposed behind an experimental flag.

A registry-backed flow gives organizations a path to use existing artifact management, access control, audit, retention, and promotion workflows for APM packages. The initial scope can focus on install-time resolution and documented HTTP API compatibility; publishing and package lifecycle management can remain future extensions.

Title: feat(install): -g should compile instructions into user-scope root context file
Body: ## Summary

`apm install -g <pkg>` deploys per-target primitives into user-scope directories (`~/.claude/skills/`,...) and writes metadata under `~/.apm/`. For `instructions` this is not enough: the harness loads them only through a root context file (`CLAUDE.md`, `AGENTS.md`, `GEMINI.md`) that `apm compile` generates, and `apm compile` has no user-scope mode.

Net effect: `apm install -g` silently installs instructions that no harness ever picks up.

##
[Middle omitted to fit model context]
.apm/ primitives -->` marker rule so a hand-authored root context file is never overwritten without consent.

Packages that contain only `skills`, `agents`, `commands`, `hooks`, or MCP already work correctly under `-g` -- compile is not on the path for those primitives.

Title: feat(deps): resolve semver constraints on git-source dependencies against repo tags
Body: ## Summary

Git-source dependencies in `apm.yml` accept only branch names, tag names,
and SHAs as `ref:` values. Marketplace dependencies (PR #1422) and
registry dependencies (PR #1471) both accept semver ranges (`^1.2.0`,
`~2.1`, `>=1.0 <2.0`). The git source is the odd one out, which forces
authors who depend on a tagged git repo to either pin to an exact tag
(losing patch-level updates) or track a moving branch (losing
determinism).

This issue
[Middle omitted to fit model context]
 resolution). Different problem
  (when to write the lockfile vs. what constraints are accepted), but
  both touch the resolution surface.
- #773 — Multi-host dependency support (lockfile identity, token
  resolution). Different concern (cross-host identity vs. semver
  routing), no coupling.

Title: feat(pack): --create-tag and --push flags to create and push release tag after --check-versions
Body: ## Summary

Add `--create-tag` and `--push` flags to `apm pack`. When
`--check-versions` succeeds, `--create-tag` creates the git tag the
check is verifying (e.g. `v1.2.0` for lockstep marketplaces, or one
per package for `per_package`). `--push` follows up by pushing the
created tag to the configured remote. Refuses to operate on a dirty
working tree, on existing tags, or when the manifest version and the
tag-to-create disagree.

##
[Middle omitted to fit model context]
 improve the release flow.
- #1474 — Authoring-repo mode (`self_install: false` on `apm pack`).
  Operates at install time (which files get deployed) while this
  issue operates at pack time (tag creation). Complementary,
  stackable, no conflict.

Title: feat(deps): apm deps why <pkg> - explain why a transitive dependency was installed
Body: ## Summary

Add `apm deps why <pkg>` — a subcommand that explains why a given
installed package is present, walking the dependency graph back to one
or more direct dependencies that pulled it in. Inspired by
`npm why`, `yarn why`, and `cargo tree -i`.

## Motivation

After running `apm install`, `apm_modules/` may contain transitive
packages that the consumer did not declare directly. When something
breaks — an unexpected MCP server, a skill that surprises the author,
a version that triggers a policy block — the
[Middle omitted to fit model context]
 `apm find` (file → package provenance). Complementary,
  orthogonal axis: #1156 answers "who put this file here?",
  `apm deps why` answers "who pulled this package in?". Both belong
  in the `apm deps` introspection surface.

Title: feat(policy): add dependencies.require_pinned_constraint to ban unbounded ranges
Body: ## Summary

Add a new boolean field `policy.dependencies.require_pinned_constraint`
to `apm.policy.yml`. When set to `true`, `apm install` (and `apm audit`)
flags any dependency whose constraint is unbounded — `*`, a bare
`>=X.Y.Z` without an upper bound, or a bare branch ref — and routes
through the existing `enforcement: warn | block | off` setting.

## Motivation

Governed installs rely on lockfiles to deliver reproducibility, but
the apm.yml manifest itself can express intent that defeats lock
[Middle omitted to fit model context]
 both (built-in pinning
  check + custom subprocess validators) once #519 lands.
- #847 — `marketplace doctor` warns when package dependencies bypass
  marketplace. Related supply-chain audit, different axis (governance
  boundary crossing vs. constraint pinning). Coexist cleanly.

Title: Epic: Strengthen install-time supply-chain integrity and policy clarity
Body: ## Summary
APM's role is the install-and-integrity layer for agent primitives (skills, agents, instructions, MCP server configs): resolve, pin, hash, lock, verify, and record what gets installed. Agent harnesses own runtime governance -- what a running agent may do once installed. This epic groups work that makes that separation explicit and deepens APM's install-time integrity guarantees.

## Why now
Two recurring sources of confusion and risk:
1. Users are unsure what `apm-policy.yml` governs. Because it exposes allow/deny lists, it can read like a generic permission system, when its
[Middle omitted to fit model context]
; APM consumes standard signatures where present.

## Definition of done
All four child issues closed; docs and policy consistently describe APM as the install-and-integrity layer; new integrity capabilities shipped with tests and CHANGELOG entries; every declarable policy key is backed by enforcement at the time it ships.

`apm-policy.yml` exposes allow/deny lists for dependencies and MCP configs. In practice this can read like a general-purpose permission system, so users ask what APM actually governs and whether it overlaps with controls their agent harness already provides. It does not overlap: APM governs installation and integrity (which sources are trusted, which versions install, whether artifacts are verified, what the lockfile records), while the agent harness governs runtime behavior.

## Problem
APM already produces a lockfile (apm.lock.yaml) with per-file SHA-256 hashes and a content-drift audit. For regulated and security-conscious teams, content hashing alone is not enough: they need a machine-readable bill of materials for what was installed, recorded provenance for where each artifact came from, and - once a signing ecosystem exists - a way to verify who produced an artifact.

[Middle omitted to fit model context]

Runtime enforcement of any kind. Building or operating signing infrastructure. APM verifies and records at install time; it does not control what a running agent may do.

## Problem
Today `apm-policy.yml` expresses governance mainly through allow/deny/require lists. Two integrity guarantees APM can enforce at install time TODAY - content-hash verification and content drift - are not first-class, declarable policy. The file under-represents what APM already enforces, which feeds the confusion about its purpose.

[Middle omitted to fit model context]

Makes APM's enforceable integrity guarantees declarable and visible in the same file teams already use, reinforcing that the policy is the install contract. With registries on the horizon, hash-pinned installs are the near-term trust anchor, so `require_hashes` is the highest-value declarable control.

As a result,all entries end up pinned to the same `ref`/`sha` instead of each resolving to its own `{name}-v{version}` tag.

In a monorepo marketplace where each package is tagged independently as `{name}-

Title: Expose `apm-version` as an import input on `shared/apm.md`
Body: ## Summary

Consumers vendor `shared/apm.md` (via `gh aw add microsoft/apm/.github/workflows/shared/apm.md`) and import it from their agentic workflows. The shared workflow pins the apm CLI version only through `microsoft/apm-action`'s built-in default — it does not expose `apm-version` as an import input. To run a newer apm CLI than the action's default, a consumer must **hand-edit the vendored `shared/apm.md`** (the `apm-version`
[Middle omitted to fit model context]
 `uses:` ref at compile time), so bumping the *action* still means editing the vendored file or pulling a newer upstream `shared/apm.md`. Exposing `apm-version` covers the common case — a newer CLI on the existing action — without that edit, since the action accepts the input regardless.

 2. Delete `my-agent.md` from the upstream repository and push the change
 3. Run `
[Middle omitted to fit model context]
 drift between the upstream package and the local deployment — the exact

The deps are genuinely transitive (the root manifest never declares them — a local-path sub-package does), but the lockfile writes them with `resolved_by: null`, so the orphan check classifies them as *direct-but-unmanifested* and flags them.

Title: [FEATURE] Enhance apm.lock.yaml to Include Installed Package Name and Version Metadata
Body: 
### Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.

APM packages require a `name` and `version` in `apm.yml`, but after `apm install` consumers cannot easily determine which package versions are installed because `apm.lock.yaml` only records repository, path, commit, and hash information.

This becomes more challenging when packages have transitive dependencies. For example, installing a Spring Boot package may automatically install additional packages such as Mermaid, documentation standards, or other shared packages. While these dependencies appear in `apm.lock.yaml`, their package versions are
[Middle omitted to fit model context]
. Developers often need to understand exactly which package versions are installed in a repository, including automatically installed dependencies.

Having package name and version information directly available in `apm.lock.yaml` would make dependency inventory, auditing, troubleshooting, and upgrade planning much easier while preserving the existing commit-based lockfile behavior.

Title: [BUG] Virtual single-file package content hashes differ across OSes due to synthetic apm.yml line endings
Body: **Describe the bug**

This breaks the portability of `apm.lock.yaml`: a lockfile produced on Windows can fail `apm install` on an Ubuntu runner with a supply-chain integrity mismatch even though the dependency commit and downloaded source file have not changed.
[Middle omitted to fit model context]
Acceptance criteria**

- A virtual single-file dependency pinned to one commit has the same `content_hash` on Windows, Linux, and macOS.
- A lockfile generated on Windows verifies without modification on an Ubuntu runner.
- Existing package-tree integrity checks for source files and binary content remain unchanged.

This was reproduced downstream with APM 0.24.0 against a lockfile generated by 0.25.0: the older CLI rewrote the newer lockfile. Refreshing dependencies or deleting caches cannot correct this because neither upgrades the running CLI.

Downstream evidence: https://gitlab.com/spiritt/ten

- The guard covers every mutating path, not only `install`.

The apm docs and source code agree on the mechanics. There is **no dedicated
policy key** for insecure transport; the docs' recommended hardening leans on
the general dependency allow list. The one soft discrepancy is that the docs
imply a policy-level control that the
[Middle omitted to fit model context]
_insecure`-aware policy check.

  experimental).

Title: [BUG] Localised git stderr breaks auth-failure classification, suppressing the token retry
Body: **Describe the bug**

`AuthResolver.is_public_github_auth_failure` classifies a failed clone by matching English signal strings against git's stderr (`"authentication failed"`, `"could not read username"`, `"repository not found"`,...). Git localises those diagnostics through gettext, and APM does not pin a locale for the git subprocesses it spawns itself.

On a machine whose locale is not English, git writes its authentication failure in the user's language. The classifier does not recognise it, and the consequence is not cosmetic: the verdict gates the **token retry** in
[Middle omitted to fit model context]

Widening the classifier's vocabulary with translated strings looks like the wrong direction — the catalogues change between git versions and cover a moving set of languages.

Title: [BUG] uninstall orphans tracked files when removed package target differs from surviving manifest targets
Body: **Describe the bug**

When a global manifest already persists one target, a later package can be installed to another target with `--target`. APM deploys that package correctly, but `apm uninstall --global` resolves cleanup targets only from the surviving manifest after removing the package.

If the removed package's deployment target is absent from that surviving target set, its files are not visited. Uninstall still exits successfully and deletes the package's manifest, module, lockfile, and deployment-ledger entries. The files become untracked orphans with no warning and cannot be cleaned by rerunning uninstall because the
[Middle omitted to fit model context]
 Phase 1 cleanup target set, derived from tracked removed-package deployments, from the Phase 2 survivor target set, derived from the surviving manifest. This report concerns per-file tracked cleanup. It is related to target-scope issues such as #2250 and the orphan symptom in #2558, but has a different reproduction and root cause.

Title: [BUG] apm lock export --timestamp accepts invalid values without error
Body: ### Bug Summary

The `--timestamp` option in `apm lock export` lacks validation for ISO 8601 formatting. Consequently, arbitrary or malformed string values are accepted without error and embedded directly into the generated CycloneDX/SPDX Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) metadata. This causes silent generation of non-compliant SBOM artifacts that fail downstream schema verification.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Execute `apm lock export` with an invalid timestamp string:
   ```bash
   apm lock export --timestamp "not-a-date"
   ```
2. Observe that the command executes successfully (exit
[Middle omitted to fit model context]


```python
def _resolve_export_timestamp(explicit: str | None,...) -> str:
    if explicit:
        return explicit  # Bypasses ISO 8601 validation
```

Validating the string via `datetime.fromisoformat()` prior to serialization will prevent silent output corruption.

Title: [BUG] Codex adapter writes ${VAR} MCP header values into static http_headers
Body: **Describe the bug**

The Codex client adapter writes an MCP server's `headers` into `~/.codex/config.toml` as `http_headers` with any `${VAR}` placeholder copied verbatim. [Middle omitted to fit model context]

Claude Code's adapter writes the identical placeholder into `headers`, where Claude Code documents environment-variable expansion, so the same dependency resolves the variable for one target and not the other.

Title: [aw] Detection Runs
Body: This issue tracks all runs where threat detection flagged problems in agentic workflows in this repository. Each workflow run that completes with a detection warning or failure posts a comment here.

<details>
<summary>What is a Detection Problem?</summary>

A detection problem occurs when the threat detection system either:
